catalog_locator: OPD 2011 p.7, 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length): STRESS'; Grammar Essentials 1992 sec. 4.1 p.24
catalog_quote: Stress is not being analyzed as phonemic, as it is not contrastive. However there are complications in discerning stress because pitch, length, and/or intensity do not function together. There is a strong tendency to stress the last syllable in any word, and in words of more than two syllables there may be one or two secondarily-stressed syllables, most frequently alternating secondary-stress and unstressed. Stress can shift with affixation and/or adjust to the stress pattern of the following word or morpheme. Reduplicated words tend to be stressed equally. ... [ɑ.ˈᵑgɑi] /ɑŋkɑ͡i/ <ankai> 'tomorrow' [ˌɑ.ᵑgɑi.ˈɛl] /ɑŋkɑ͡i ɛl/ <ankaiel> 'tomorrow-(dep.cl.)' In the first example, the word in isolation, the stress is on the second and last syllable. However when it is followed by the clitic –el ... the stress moves from the second syllable to the clitic, with some secondary stress on the fir…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (non-phonemic stress, strong tendency to word-final primary stress, alternating secondaries leftward, rightward shift onto clitics such as -el, pervasive exceptions) rests on the primary fieldworker's own phonology statement (OPD 2011, p.7, quote confirmed verbatim) and her 123-pp grammar sketch (1992, sec. 4.1 p.25, quote confirmed; record locator says p.24, off by one). These are the only first-hand descriptions of Kombio in Glottolog/OLAC; the only unheld 'grammar' (Yi 2008) is an unpublished WALS-sourced sketch. The dictionary downloaded now (418 pp, stress-marked IPA) independently supports final stress as the typical pattern (~72% of marked polysyllables) with many exceptions, matching the exceptions statement='pervasive'. no reclassification needed; optionally fix the Grammar Essentials locator to p.25.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: No general stress section in the introduction (it defers to the OPD), but entries carry stress-marked IPA and notes treating final stress as the 'typical' pattern and -el as attracting stress. A rough machine tally of the stress-marked polysyllabic transcriptions in the text layer gives 1818/2528 (72%) final primary stress, 446 penult, 264 other — consistent with 'strong tendency' to final stress with pervasive exceptions.
sources.locator: Entry-level phonetic notes, e.g. p.178 s.v. ntamai [ˈⁿda.mai]: 'Notice the stress change - accent on first syllable here whereas in other dialect and in typical stress patterns, accent would be on last syllable'; p.238 s.v. sukupel [ˌsu.ku.ˈɸɛl]: 'Note that the stress changes when the -el suffix is added'; intro p.7 refers readers to the OPD for phonology.
sources.note: Same fieldworker's 4250-entry dictionary with stress-marked IPA per entry; gives lexical-scale evidence for the 'strong tendency' to final stress and the exception rate behind our 'pervasive exceptions' flag. downloaded now; confirms.
